title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-wip-2
content:
Purpose:
This document captures the benchmarking harness and methodology we use to measure throughput for the serving runtime. It focuses on repeatability, realistic load generation, warmup strategy (KV/ATTN cache), and profiling steps to identify bottlenecks. This is a working doc; decisions here should be validated by CI runs and linked dashboards.

High-level goals:
- Produce repeatable throughput measurements (tokens/sec, sequences/sec) across hardware configurations and builds.
- Separate steady-state performance from cold-start and warmup behaviour.
- Provide a reproducible harness for A/B testing runtime changes and kernel/quantization variants.
- Capture metrics needed for cost/latency trade-offs (p50/p95/p99 latency, tail-queued requests, GPU/CPU utilization).

Environment best-practices (reproducibility):
- Use pinned Docker images and recorded infra provisioning scripts. Record CUDA, cuDNN, driver, and kernel versions in the run metadata.
- Set CPU governor to performance and pin benchmark processes to dedicated cores. Isolate NUMA nodes and use hugepages if applicable.
- Stop non-essential services and cron jobs; run inside dedicated benchmark VM/container.
- Fix random seeds for model initialization paths that affect request-time behaviour (e.g., dropout, sampling).
- Use the same model artifacts (quantization files, kernel caches) across runs; record SHA256 of model files.
- For GPU determinism, set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 only for debug runs; production runs should use normal async execution but record stream concurrency config.

Workload design and input datasets:
- Realistic workload distribution is essential. Two approaches:
  1) Production trace replay: sample real requests from production logs (anonymize PII), preserving sequence length distribution, prompt prefixes, and tokenization behaviour.
  2) Synthetic mixes: create request mixes that represent expected product workloads (short chat messages, medium completions, long docs).
- Record the length distribution bucket definitions (e.g., short: 1-32 tokens, medium: 33-128, long: 129-1024) and the fraction of workload in each bucket.
- Keep prompt diversity: repeated identical prompts can inflate caching effects; include both repeated and unique prefixes to exercise KV cache behavior.

Load generator configuration patterns:
- Arrival patterns:
  - Constant QPS: ideal when measuring max sustained throughput at a fixed concurrency.
  - Poisson (exponential inter-arrival): models more natural web traffic.
  - Step/ramp: ramp up to target QPS over X seconds to avoid initial overload.
  - Spike test: send sudden high QPS bursts to observe graceful degradation/fallbacks.
  - Soak test: long-duration runs (hours) to detect memory leaks and accumulation effects.
- Concurrency controls:
  - max_inflight_requests: cap of concurrent requests allowed.
  - per-worker concurrency (for multi-worker setups) to bind threads/streams.
- Example loadgen config (recommended defaults for initial runs):
  - ramp_up: 60s
  - warmup_requests: 200 (see warmup section)
  - steady_window: 300s (measurement window)
  - runs_per_config: 5
  - discard_first_run: true
  - arrival_pattern: poisson
  - seed: 42 (for synthetic workload generators)

Warmup strategy (critical for steady-state):
- Purpose: populate KV caches, populate compiled kernel caches, and warm GPU kernels to steady thermal/perf state.
- Warmup primitives:
  - KV pre-seed: For models with KV caching, send a set of long context requests that exercise typical prefixes. The goal is to ensure the server has filled commonly used KV slots.
  - Kernel cache warm: Execute model forward passes with a set of representative lengths and batch sizes to populate JIT/compiled caches.
  - Thermal/stability: short idle -> warm pipeline by sending sustained low-rate traffic for X seconds to stabilize clock governors.
- Recommended warmup procedure:
  1) Start with a 60s ramp to warm up the system.
  2) Send warmup_requests=200 distributed across length buckets; ensure at least 20% of them are long requests.
  3) Wait an additional 30s idle to allow metrics exporters to catch up.
  4) Start steady measurement window.
- Notes: For experiments targeting cold-start performance, use a separate test that starts from a freshly restarted runtime and records startup latency metrics.

Instrumentation and metrics to collect:
- Request-level: request_id, request_size_tokens, response_tokens, start_ts, end_ts, queuing_time, server_processing_time, backend_gpu_time, status_code.
- Aggregates: total_tokens, tokens_per_sec, sequences_per_sec, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, mean latency, stddev.
- Resource metrics: GPU utilization, GPU memory, GPU SM occupancy (if available), PCIe throughput, CPU utilization per core, host memory RSS, context switches, disk IO, NIC throughput.
- System traces: use Nsight Systems or perf when investigating low-level bottlenecks; collect flamegraphs for CPU and GPU kernels when needed.
- Serving-specific: batch sizes observed, KV cache hit rate, effective batching latency breakdown (batch_wait + compute).
- Exporter notes: tag metrics with run_id, build_sha, model_sha, hw_config, and loadgen_config. Persist raw request logs and aggregated metrics to S3/GCS for post-run analysis.

Profiling workflow when throughput regresses or is suboptimal:
1) Reproduce the regression with the harness and record detailed metrics. Compare to baseline run.
2) Capture per-request traces for slow/queued requests and aggregate by source-length-bucket. Look for changes in batching behavior.
3) Use GPU profiling tools (Nsight Systems, nvprof where available) to inspect kernel launch rates, kernel durations, and SM utilization.
4) Capture CPU flamegraphs (perf/FlameGraph) to find scheduler contention or Python-level bottlenecks (GIL, serialization).
5) Inspect kernel selection logs and quantization code paths. Changes to chosen kernels (e.g., fallback to slower kernels) often explain regressions.
6) Examine memory pressure: paging, allocator growth, and fragmentation. Look for OOM or increased GC frequency.
7) If hardware-level variance suspected, run microbenchmarks (memory copy, matmul) to validate device behaviour.

Statistical methodology and repeatability:
- Repeat each config N times (default N=5) and report median plus interquartile range. Discard the first run by default to avoid warmup noise.
- Use bootstrap sampling to estimate 95% confidence intervals for throughput metrics when distributions are skewed.
- When comparing two builds, run paired experiments (alternating runs between A and B) to reduce time-varying environmental noise.
- Flag differences as meaningful only when effect size exceeds noise band (e.g., change > 2 * stddev or outside 95% CI).

Failure modes and why tests can be flaky:
- Non-deterministic background processes on host (cron, monitoring agents).
- Driver/kernel mismatches or automatic driver updates on test hosts.
- Thermal throttling from previous runs—ensure cooling windows between long soak tests.
- Fluctuating multi-tenant noisy neighbors on cloud VMs. Use dedicated instances for critical comparisons.
- Randomized kernel selection or scheduling heuristics tuned for latency may change throughput. Record policy flags used by runtime.

Output artifacts and naming conventions:
- Each run emits a run manifest JSON (run_id, timestamp, build_sha, model_sha, hw_config, loadgen_config, warmup_config).
- Metrics file: metrics-run-{run_id}.csv (flat table: timestamp, metric_name, value, tags).
- Raw request log: requests-run-{run_id}.ndjson (one JSON-per-line request-level data).
- Profiling artifacts: profile-run-{run_id}-nsys.qdrep, perf.{run_id}.data, flamegraph-{run_id}.svg.
- Store artifacts under: s3://redwood-benchmarks/{model}/{build_sha}/{run_id}/

Automation and CI integration:
- Add a nightly benchmark job that runs a small battery of canonical configs and updates baseline dashboards.
- For PRs touching runtime, provide a lightweight smoke throughput job that compares against main, and a link to a reproducible run.
- Keep a curated set of canonical inputs (short/medium/long) checked into bench-data/ with checksums.

Open questions and next steps (action items):
- Decide on default warmup_requests and whether to tie warmup duration to token counts instead of request counts. (Owner: Priya)
- Add automated kernel-version recording to run manifests (Owner: Riley).
- Create a standard trace anonymization pipeline for production replay (Owner: Daniel).
- Add GPU SM-level occupancy metrics to the standard exporter (Owner: Maya).

Appendix: quick checklist for a clean benchmark run:
- [ ] Provision dedicated host with recorded image.
- [ ] Pin CPU governor and isolate cores.
- [ ] Pull pinned Docker image and model artifact by SHA.
- [ ] Start exporter and verify scraping.
- [ ] Run warmup sequence and confirm KV cache hits > expected threshold.
- [ ] Run N repeated measurement windows and archive outputs.
